title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch-plywood speaker cabinet prototype was built in June 1972 at the Alembic shop by Rick Turner and Ron Wickersham labeled “COSMIC 672” in red; similar to other Alembic PA cabinets built for the Dead in 1972 and 1973. Cabinet also contained a JBL K140 Speaker for the piano that was converted into a bass cabinet for Phil Lesh with handprinted “Parish Side.” Steve Parish was stage manager for the 1974 Grateful Dead and a member of the band’s road crew.   This cabinet is one of Stanley “Bear’” Owsley’s first hifi creations that had individual Altec and JBL speakers for each instrument, driven by McIntosh power amps—and that debuted at the Cow Palace on March 23, 1974.  In practice, cabinets such as the “COSMIC 672” were the pieces the crew listened to, measured, and retuned as they worked out how to eliminate distortion, remove the need for stage monitors, and give each player a dedicated, full range PA of their own.  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.    Speaker cabinet: 30 ¾ x 15 x 14 ¾ in.  Road case: 34 ½ x 18 ½ x 16 ¼ in.

description_block: This cabinet was built for the Grateful Dead’s 1974 “Wall of Sound” and originally housed a speaker that carried Phil Lesh’s bass or for piano. In 1991, the cabinet was acquired by Simon Babbs, son of Ken Babbs who was a member of the Merry Pranksters and close collaborator of founder Ken Kesey. The cabinet was moved to Ken Kesey’s farm in Oregon where it was highly modified and painted red and white and then actively used by the Merry Pranksters Band. Photographs from early 1990s Fourth of July parties show the red Wall of Sound derived cabinets on the back of Kesey’s stage truck, with Ken and his wife Faye performing in front of them.  Cabinet has various stickers affixed including a “Free the Hostages,” dating back to the Iran Hostage Crisis which took place from 1979 to 1981; “Hard Truckers” circular sticker from the 1970s and 1980s. On the top of the cabinet is the handwritten notation “Property of Simon Babbs & Tom Bassett.”  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.    Speaker cabinet: 19 ¼ x 16 ½ x 30 in.  Road case: 22 x 19 ¾ x 33 ½ in.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch plywood cabinet with JBL K120 and JBL 2202A loudspeakers, built specifically for keyboardist Keith Godchaux’s piano channel and engineered to capture the instantaneous, vertical hammerstrike of a grand piano. Cabinet was built in early 1974 by members of the Grateful Dead road crew—known in later years as Hard Truckers—in collaboration with the Alembic shop in San Francisco.   During the 1974 Wall of Sound tour in the United States, the cabinet was part of the dedicated piano cluster feeding Keith Godchaux’s grand piano. When the system was scaled and adapted for European dates later that year, piano and bass cabinets like this one traveled with the band.  “209” handwritten in marker on the back and right side, consistent with Wall of Sound box numbering practices. “PIANO” hand-stenciled in blue paint on the back toward the bottom (partially over sprayed with white paint), identifying this box as part of the piano array. On the JBL K120, the interior paper cone bears the signature “Kevin Konecky” in white marker. Konecky was a Wall of Sound audio engineer who worked closely with Owsley “Bear” Stanley on design, setup, and nightly operation. On the interior frame of the JBL 2202A, the name “Stereo Doctor” is written in white marker, echoing the nickname used for Owsley “Bear” Stanley in his capacity as the system’s chief sound architect. A period “Grim Reaper” violinist sticker appears on the right side of the cabinet. This image, designed by Alton Kelley, was used on Grateful Dead tour stickers circa 1973 and is frequently associated with the Dead’s own stage and road gear from that era.  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.    Speaker: 21 x 16 ½ x 26 in.  Road case: 25 ½ x 19 ¾ x 29 ½ in.

description_block: 29 ¾ x 20 ¼ in. Original mechanical artwork for Fleetwood Mac’s iconic 1977 masterpiece,  . The artwork featuring black and white photographs by Herbert Worthington III. The mechanical artwork comprises two separate pieces of illustration board; each containing two photographs.   First illustration board comprises the front cover featuring Mick Fleetwood and Stevie Nicks striking the now iconic pose. Nicks in her supernatural “Rhiannon” persona. Mick Fleetwood wears black waistcoat, matching trousers, long stockings and ballet slippers. Fleetwood wearing his now infamous wooden balls with chains hanging from his waist that Fleetwood yanked out of a toilet tank years earlier and became his Talisman. Board also features back cover artwork with Worthington’s contact sheets and collage of various photographs, including outtakes from the session; conveying casualness and intimacy not typically used on album art. Overlay of onionskin paper with notes in red marker and black and blue ballpoint.   Second illustration board featuring gatefold artwork; two black and white photographs including outtakes from the session; comprising collage and contact prints by Worthington. description_block: Phil Lesh Bass Cabinet with JBL D140F Loudspeaker with birch construction built in the San Francisco Bay Area by the Grateful Dead road crew (later known as Hard Truckers) in collaboration with Alembic. Assigned to Phil Lesh's bass array and matched to his famous Osiris bass guitar. Lesh debuted his Osiris bass on stage 16 June 1974, and he played it at nearly every show through 1979, including footage shot at Cornell University on 8 May 1977, the Great Pyramid concerts, and the closing of Winterland. This cabinet was purpose-built for that specific instrument.  Lesh's bass setup featured a custom quadraphonic, six channel instrument that sent each of its four strings to a separate channel. This cabinet was one of the dedicated low frequency boxes in that bass array.  A New Riders of the Purple Sage sticker on the cabinet side places its use in 1974, when the New Riders regularly opened for the Dead and shared access to the “Wall of Sound.”  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.    Speaker cabinet: 25 ¼ x 20 x 28 ½ in.   Road case: 29 x 23 ¾ x 32 ½ in.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch plywood cabinet from the Grateful Dead’s “Wall of Sound” speaker system for Keith Godchaux’s acoustic piano. The cabinet features a pair of JBL D120F loudspeakers—high efficiency, 12 in. Alnico drivers codeveloped by JBL and Fender.   This cabinet was built in early 1974 by Alembic workers in conjunction with the Grateful Dead road crew—later known as Hard Truckers—in the San Francisco Bay Area. The materials, joinery, custom brackets, and removable baffle match other documented Wall of Sound boxes. It was numbered “208” and stenciled “PIANO,” marking it as part of Keith’s array.   Back of frame carries “G.D.” (Grateful Dead), “Ram…,” (Referring to the band’s roadie Laurence Shurtliff aka “Ramrod.” “Lumier,” “S.F.,” referring to the Lumiere Theatre and the date “32374,” the day the completed Wall of Sound debuted at the Cow Palace in Daly City, California.  On 23 March 1974, the fully realized “Wall of Sound” made its touring debut at the Cow Palace. The “32374” marking on one of the D120F frames aligns with that rollout. The piano cabinets—including No. 208—were used behind and above the band as part of the modular piano array, giving Keith Godchaux his channel. When the system was adapted for the European leg later that year, piano and bass cabinets like this one were part of the traveling inventory.

title: The Beatles
description_block: This 10 ½ in. EMI master tape is an effects tape that was used during the overdubbing and mixing stages of the album. It contains nearly 22 minutes of takes/tracks of songs written by John Lennon and recorded toward the end of the recording process. Included on the tape are the following recordings:  1. Recorded 8 October 1968 – An unreleased take of “I’m So Tired,” focusing on John’s vocals. Includes Lennon’s count in (1-2-3) and a single tracked (not double, like the release) alternate take with Lennon’s vocal in front. Ringo’s drums are way in the background with Mellotron keyboard and no rhythm guitar. Includes four full takes and four with tape roll-back.  2. Recorded 8 October 1968 – Unreleased backing track for “I’m So Tired” – Includes unused George Harrison guitar solo “track” meant for “I’m So Tired” and never released. This solo lays on top of the Mellotron and Ringo’s drums. This can be heard faintly on a version of “I’m So Tired” in the 50th Anniversary box set; the entire backing track in full studio quality included herein.  3. Recorded 25 September 1968 – Unreleased backing track for “Happiness is a Warm Gun” – This unused backing track includes Mellotron, Ringo Starr’s drums, and George Harrison guitar solos, piano, and tambourine. Includes one full take and two with tape roll back.  4. Recorded 29 August 1968 – Unreleased backing track for “Dear Prudence” – This unused backing track includes the backing harmonies (“aaaah, ooohs”) and hand clapping. Lennon’s vocals can be heard in the background.

description_block: This cabinet was built for the Grateful Dead’s 1974 Wall of Sound and originally housed a speaker that carried Phil Lesh’s bass or piano. In 1991, the cabinet was acquired by Simon Babbs, son of Ken Babbs who was a member of the Merry Pranksters and close collaborator of founder Ken Kesey. The cabinet was moved to the Kesey farm in Oregon where it was highly modified and painted red and white and then actively used by the Merry Pranksters Band. description_block: This birch-plywood speaker cabinet prototype was built in June 1972 at the Alembic shop by Rick Turner and Ron Wickersham labeled “COSMIC 672” in red; similar to other Alembic PA cabinets built for the Dead in 1972 and 1973. Cabinet also contained a JBL K140 Speaker for the piano that was converted into a bass cabinet for Phil Lesh with handprinted “Parish Side.” Steve Parish was stage manager for the 1974 Grateful Dead and a member of the band’s road crew.   This cabinet is one of Stanley “Bear’” Owsley’s first hifi creations that had individual Altec and JBL speakers for each instrument, driven by McIntosh power amps—and that debuted at the Cow Palace on March 23, 1974.  In practice, cabinets such as the “COSMIC 672” were the pieces the crew listened to, measured, and retuned as they worked out how to eliminate distortion, remove the need for stage monitors, and give each player a dedicated, full range PA of their own.  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.    Speaker cabinet: 30 ¾ x 15 x 14 ¾ in.  Road case: 34 ½ x 18 ½ x 16 ¼ in.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch plywood cabinet from the Grateful Dead’s “Wall of Sound” speaker system for Keith Godchaux’s acoustic piano. The cabinet features a pair of JBL D120F loudspeakers—high efficiency, 12 in. Alnico drivers codeveloped by JBL and Fender.   This cabinet was built in early 1974 by Alembic workers in conjunction with the Grateful Dead road crew—later known as Hard Truckers—in the San Francisco Bay Area. The materials, joinery, custom brackets, and removable baffle match other documented Wall of Sound boxes. It was numbered “208” and stenciled “PIANO,” marking it as part of Keith’s array.   Back of frame carries “G.D.” (Grateful Dead), “Ram…,” (Referring to the band’s roadie Laurence Shurtliff aka “Ramrod.” “Lumier,” “S.F.,” referring to the Lumiere Theatre and the date “32374,” the day the completed Wall of Sound debuted at the Cow Palace in Daly City, California.  On 23 March 1974, the fully realized “Wall of Sound” made its touring debut at the Cow Palace. The “32374” marking on one of the D120F frames aligns with that rollout. The piano cabinets—including No. 208—were used behind and above the band as part of the modular piano array, giving Keith Godchaux his channel. When the system was adapted for the European leg later that year, piano and bass cabinets like this one were part of the traveling inventory.

description_block: This 10 ½ in. EMI master tape is an effects tape that was used during the overdubbing and mixing stages of the album. It contains nearly 22 minutes of takes/tracks of songs written by John Lennon and recorded toward the end of the recording process. Included on the tape are the following recordings:  1. Recorded 8 October 1968 – An unreleased take of “I’m So Tired,” focusing on John’s vocals. Includes Lennon’s count in (1-2-3) and a single tracked (not double, like the release) alternate take with Lennon’s vocal in front. Ringo’s drums are way in the background with Mellotron keyboard and no rhythm guitar. Includes four full takes and four with tape roll-back.  2. Recorded 8 October 1968 – Unreleased backing track for “I’m So Tired” – Includes unused George Harrison guitar solo “track” meant for “I’m So Tired” and never released. This solo lays on top of the Mellotron and Ringo’s drums. This can be heard faintly on a version of “I’m So Tired” in the 50th Anniversary box set; the entire backing track in full studio quality included herein.  3. Recorded 25 September 1968 – Unreleased backing track for “Happiness is a Warm Gun” – This unused backing track includes Mellotron, Ringo Starr’s drums, and George Harrison guitar solos, piano, and tambourine. Includes one full take and two with tape roll back.  4. Recorded 29 August 1968 – Unreleased backing track for “Dear Prudence” – This unused backing track includes the backing harmonies (“aaaah, ooohs”) and hand clapping. title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch plywood cabinet with JBL K120 and JBL 2202A loudspeakers, built specifically for keyboardist Keith Godchaux’s piano channel and engineered to capture the instantaneous, vertical hammerstrike of a grand piano. Cabinet was built in early 1974 by members of the Grateful Dead road crew—known in later years as Hard Truckers—in collaboration with the Alembic shop in San Francisco.   During the 1974 Wall of Sound tour in the United States, the cabinet was part of the dedicated piano cluster feeding Keith Godchaux’s grand piano. When the system was scaled and adapted for European dates later that year, piano and bass cabinets like this one traveled with the band.  “209” handwritten in marker on the back and right side, consistent with Wall of Sound box numbering practices. “PIANO” hand-stenciled in blue paint on the back toward the bottom (partially over sprayed with white paint), identifying this box as part of the piano array. On the JBL K120, the interior paper cone bears the signature “Kevin Konecky” in white marker. Konecky was a Wall of Sound audio engineer who worked closely with Owsley “Bear” Stanley on design, setup, and nightly operation. On the interior frame of the JBL 2202A, the name “Stereo Doctor” is written in white marker, echoing the nickname used for Owsley “Bear” Stanley in his capacity as the system’s chief sound architect. A period “Grim Reaper” violinist sticker appears on the right side of the cabinet. This image, designed by Alton Kelley, was used on Grateful Dead tour stickers circa 1973 and is frequently associated with the Dead’s own stage and road gear from that era.  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.    Speaker: 21 x 16 ½ x 26 in.  Road case: 25 ½ x 19 ¾ x 29 ½ in.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This cabinet was built for the Grateful Dead’s 1974 Wall of Sound and originally housed a speaker that carried Phil Lesh’s bass or piano. In 1991, the cabinet was acquired by Simon Babbs, son of Ken Babbs who was a member of the Merry Pranksters and close collaborator of founder Ken Kesey. The cabinet was moved to the Kesey farm in Oregon where it was highly modified and painted red and white and then actively used by the Merry Pranksters Band. Photographs from early 1990s Fourth of July parties show the red Wall of Sound derived cabinets on the back of Kesey’s stage truck, with Ken and his wife Faye performing in front of them.  Cabinet has various stickers affixed including BOAC (British Airways) for air cargo for the 1974 European tour. Hand printed “PIANO” on back and “13.” “K140” signifying that cabinet originally contained a JBL K140 piano or bass speaker for Phil Lesh. “Parish” referring to the band’s stage manager Steve Parish. On the top of the cabinet is the handwritten notation “Property of Simon Babbs & Tom Bassett.”  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.    Speaker cabinet: 19 ¼ x 16 ½ x 30 in.  Road case: 22 x 19 ¾ x 33 ½ in.

title: Fleetwood Mac
description_block: 29 ¾ x 20 ¼ in. Original mechanical artwork for Fleetwood Mac’s iconic 1977 masterpiece,  . The artwork featuring black and white photographs by Herbert Worthington III. Design and layout by Desmond Strobel and calligraphy by Larry Vigon of Vigon Nahas Vigon. The mechanical artwork comprises two separate pieces of illustration board; each containing two photographs.   First illustration board comprises the front cover featuring Mick Fleetwood and Stevie Nicks striking the now iconic pose. Nicks in her supernatural “Rhiannon” persona. Mick Fleetwood wears black waistcoat, matching trousers, long stockings and ballet slippers. Fleetwood wearing his now infamous wooden balls with chains hanging from his waist that Fleetwood yanked out of a toilet tank years earlier and became his Talisman. Board also features back cover artwork with Worthington’s contact sheets and collage of various photographs, including outtakes from the session; conveying casualness and intimacy not typically used on album art. Overlay of onionskin paper with notes in red marker and black and blue ballpoint.   Second illustration board featuring gatefold artwork; two black and white photographs including outtakes from the session; comprising collage and contact prints by Worthington. With onion skin paper with notes in brown marker and black ballpoint, detailing retouching and printers instructions for Warner Brothers’ production department.
